newsitem.title: USA: U.S. defense chief "disgusted" by Marine brutality.
newsitem.headline: U.S. defense chief "disgusted" by Marine brutality.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Cohen on Friday condemned bloody initiation incidents in which U.S. Marine trainees had medals pounded into their chests, saying he will not tolerate brutality in the ranks.
"I am disturbed and disgusted by the treatment of young Marines in the hazing incident," Cohen said at his first news conference as recently confirmed U.S. defence chief.

He referred to bloody training rituals involving Marine trainees in 1991 and 1993, films of which were leaked to television networks and aired on Friday. Marine leaders also condemned the incidents and are conducting an investigation.

"Abuse such as this has no place in any branch of the United States military," Cohen said. "... You can be sure that I intend to enforce a strict policy of zero tolerance of hazing, of sexual harassment and of racism."

The broadcast newsfilm, taken at a training camp for Marine paratroopers in Camp Lejeune, North Carolina, showed Marines writhing and crying out in pain as others pounded the spiked medals into their chests through tee-shirts.

Cohen said he understood there had been about 80 incidents of hazing uncovered in the Marine Corps in the past three to five years, although it remained to be determined how widespread such practices were in the U.S. military.
Gen. John Shalikashvili, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff who joined Cohen, added: "One incident is too many."
Cohen said high-pressure training designed to toughen recruits and weld them into a fighting forces "can cross the line into this type of abuse" and that cannot be condoned.
He and Shalikashvili promised the incidents would be fully investigated but said they could not comment in more detail for fear of prejudicing any cases that might be developed for prosecution.

The videotaped Marine ritual, marking completion of preparation for parachute duty, is the second recent controversy to cloud U.S. military training programmes. The Army is investigating widespread accusations by female recruits of harassment and rape by male drill instructors.

"I am outraged that Marines would participate in such disgusting behaviour. There is absolutely no excuse for this type of behaviour," the Marine Corps commandant, Gen. Charles Krulak, said in a statement on Friday.
He said the corps, which prides itself on its toughness, had learned of the videotaped incidents earlier this month and prompt action was taken to investigate and end such practices.
Calling the hazing "shocking and degrading," corps officials said the five-year time limit had expired for judicial punishment such as jail for trainers involved in the 1991 incident.
They said courts-martial and even penalties of jail were still a possibility in the 1993 incident and any active trainers found to be responsible could be dismissed from the corps in either incident.

Most of the Marines on the 1991 videotape have been identified and an initial assessment indicates that nine remain on active duty, the Marines said. The service was still working on identifying those in the 1993 tape.

"I am committed to ridding the corps of such heinous behaviour and to ensuring that Marines treat each other with dignity, care and concern," said Krulak, who designated Lt. Gen. Charles Wilhelm, commander of Marine forces in the Atlantic region, to head the investigation.
